asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Welcome House - The Chestnuts - Archived
asgRatings.name: Care Homes
asgRatings.commentary:
We carried out this inspection to Welcome House – The Chestnuts on 12 August and 27 August 2025 as the registered manager was not available on our first day of inspection. Welcome House – The Chestnuts is a care home providing personal care and accommodation for up to 15 people with a mental health diagnosis. At the time of our inspection, 14 people were living at the service, all of whom required the regulated activity of personal care.

At our last inspection, we identified breaches of regulation in relation to safe care and treatment and good governance. At this inspection, we found those shortfalls had not been improved on.

We continued to find poor governance within the service and people were not engaging in meaningful activities or being given the opportunity to live fulfilling lives. Staff were not thinking holistically about people’s needs, wishes or goals and supporting people to work through these to regain or retain their independence.

There was a poor culture within the service where leaders and staff had failed to recognise an ongoing detrimental impact on people’s safety and well-being. Staff did not always understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

Management had failed to recognise where safeguarding incidents had occurred and as such had not reported these appropriately to the relevant authorities. In addition, where accidents and incidents occurred, although action was taken at the time, learning from these was not embedded robustly to help reduce future incidents.

Management had not ensured people lived in an environment that was clean, well presented, safe and fit for its purpose. We found people’s home was dirty and contained areas that could harbour bacteria. In addition, the rear garden of the service was littered with unsuitable items which demonstrated a lack of respect and dignity towards people.

Management had not ensured there were sufficient staff on duty each day to enable people to go out with staff on an individual or impromptu basis. The provider allowed staff to work exceptionally long hours without a break meaning people were cared for by staff who may be tired and as a result may not provide high-quality care.

Staff did not follow good medicine management practices or ensure people’s care plans were accurate and up to date in relation to people’s health care needs.

Governance arrangements were not robust and shortfalls were not identified through audits and staff were not always following the principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

Staff, however told us they received good training, supervision and support from the registered manager and it was evident they knew people well. Staff had ensured some people’s lives had improved through their care and dedication, and where people needed the input of external healthcare professionals this was sought promptly and appropriately.

The service was in breach of 7 legal requirements in relation to person centred care, safe care and treatment, safeguarding service users from abuse and improper treatment, good governance, staffing, treating people with dignity and respect, and failure to submit notifications of incidents.

This service is being placed in special measures. The purpose of special measures is to ensure that services providing inadequate care make significant improvements. Special measures provide a framework within which we use our enforcement powers in response to inadequate care and provide a timeframe within which providers must improve the quality of the care they provide. In instances where CQC have decided to take civil or criminal enforcement action against a provider, we will publish this information on our website after any representations and/ or appeals have been concluded.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing badly and we've taken action against the person or organisation that runs it.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience: People told us staff were kind towards them, however they felt they did not always have the opportunity to go out when they wished to, particularly in the evening or participate in and learn day to day skills, such as baking or cooking.Most people said they were happy living at the service and that they felt safe, although we did hear from 2 people who told us they had felt less safe since one person had moved in with them. People also said they were not consulted as to who moved in and were not given the opportunity to express their views when decisions were made that affected them, such as the location of the smoking area.People had the opportunity to participate in in-house meetings where they could give their feedback on the food or activities and as a result of one of these, an additional option was added to the daily menu.People’s lives were very insular with little evidence of them going out or attending activities that were meaningful to them and their goals or ambitions were not always pursued by staff.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring

Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Good. At this assessment the rating has changed to Inadequate. This meant people were not treated with compassion and there were breaches of dignity; staff caring attitudes had significant shortfalls.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to treating people with dignity and respect.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager and staff did not promote people’s independence. One person said, “I can retain some independence where I can, but I would like to think I could do some cooking.”

Although people were involved in their care plans, due to the staffing arrangements at the service some people did not have the choice of when they could go out, and they could not go out spontaneously. There were no opportunities for people to take part in social activities during the evening. One person mentioned they would have liked to visit the restaurant down the road, but said they were unable to go out at night.

Staff said people had keyworkers (a designated member of the staff team who advocates for the person and works towards goals with them). They told us, “We have keyworkers for people. They have chats with people to find out what they like or don’t like (for example, meal choices). They sit with the person and speak to them about what should be in their care plan.” But there was no evidence that these key workers supported people to have choice and control over their lives.

There was a lack of consistent approach to support people to retain or regain their independence. Staff did the ironing and supported people to clean their rooms, rather than encouraging them to do this themselves. A staff member said, “We encourage service users to wash up. If there are vegetables to be peeled they can join in.” But this was the extent of independent daily living skills that staff involved people in. In addition when we asked staff how people were supported to achieve their independence, they were unsure how to answer this other than to say, “By meeting their care needs.”

Although the kitchen door remained open throughout the day, we did not observe anyone assisting with lunch preparation or making their own drinks. Lunch, despite being a simple dish, was prepared entirely by staff and afterwards the tables and kitchen were cleared by the provider’s quality assurance manager who was visiting on the day. One person told us, “I don’t believe I am allowed in the kitchen. I would like to make my own drink as sometimes they forget to put milk in it and I don’t like it.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Although staff demonstrated a kind and caring approach, people were not treated with respect, privacy or dignity.

The garden at the service had unsuitable items in it which demonstrated a lack of dignity to people’s home environment. Staff had not considered whether people wanted these unsightly items in their garden and how it may impact them on a day-to-day basis. Staff said, “People are not interested in the garden. We have tried to get them involved, but instead the staff just cut down the weeds.” However, staff had not considered that people may not wish to be involved in the garden because it was uninviting and uncared for. When we visited on the second day, we found the garden had been tidied up and the items removed.

In addition, a ‘smoking’ area has been established to the side of the premises. This was used regularly throughout the day as many people living at the service smoked. But staff had not considered one person whose bedroom was adjacent to this smoking area. They told us, “The smell of smoke doesn’t always bother me, but I don’t like the noise. I can’t read my book because it is too noisy (with staff and people chatting in the smoking area). It's not all day, but it is often.” The person confirmed they had not been consulted on the location of the smoking area.However, the registered manager told us that the smoking area had been established prior to this person moving in and they had been given a choice of rooms at the time.

At other times of the day we heard staff interacting with people in a kind way and people told us staff were caring towards them. One person said, “Staff are kind to me.” A second told us, “The staff are kind and generally everyone is nice here.” It was one person’s birthday on the first day of our visit and staff had organised a cake, everyone sang happy birthday and cake was passed around to people.

Staff respected people’s privacy. They told us some people locked their bedroom doors when they were not in their rooms. At these times staff would respect the person’s choice to do this and only enter a person’s room after asking for permission. A staff member said, “If people are out they lock their doors and we don’t go into their rooms.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always listen to and understand people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff did not always respond to people’s needs in the moment or act to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress.

We read of the numerous incidents which occurred in the service, some of which resulted in people being harmed or feeling unsafe. Despite this, the registered manager had not considered these as potential safeguarding concerns and as such reported them to the local authority safeguarding team to enable them to take any appropriate action. This meant people experienced unnecessary distress.

Yet there were some examples where people’s needs had been responded to. For example, where one person was accompanied to the local temple to pray, and another person who wished to go out on the afternoon of our second visit and the registered manager ensured they were able to do this immediately they mentioned it.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff did not treat people as individuals or make sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences.

Staff were not able to tell us about people goals and aspirations. We spoke to one staff member about a person asking how the person was supported with their addiction. We were told, “Staff make sure she’s engaged so her mind does not have time to wander.” When we asked if there was any structured approach or if the person had any independence, goals or ambitions, we were told there was nothing in place. The staff member said, “We sit and we talk to her. I am not sure (about independence, etc). She has made breakfast before.”

Staff did not always consider people’s cultural and unique backgrounds or protected characteristics. Although there was information about a person’s religious beliefs in their care plan, there was nothing else around their sexuality, cultural or ethnicity needs and preferences. Some people were from a distinct ethnic group however this had not been identified in their care plan. Staff did however accompany one person to a temple so they could pray which met their religious preferences.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always care about and promote the wellbeing of their staff or themselves.

We reviewed the rotas over a 4-week period as the registered manager explained that they and the deputy manager took responsibility for being on-call on alternate weeks. Due to the registered manager’s annual leave, the deputy manager worked 3 consecutive weeks Monday to Friday at the service (completing 53, 50 and 47 hours respectively) while also being on call for the full 7 days each week. As a result, during this 3-week period the deputy manager had no time fully away from work for rest or relaxation. Additionally, at the end of July the registered manager worked 55 hours in the service Monday to Friday while also being on call for 7 consecutive days. Extended working weeks with no full rest days greatly increases the risk of exhaustion and also the risk of mistakes occurring.

Staff however told us they felt supported. One staff member said, “The manager does support me. She encourages me to be involved in the care plans which is good development for me.” A second staff member told us, “The manager’s door is always open. They gave me time to speak about a recent incident and suggested I take time out if I needed it. I felt very supported. If I needed more structured support such as counselling, I am certain it would be available for me.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective

Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Good. At this assessment the rating has changed to Requires Improvement. This meant the effectiveness of people’s care, treatment and support did not always achieve good outcomes or was inconsistent.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to people’s safe care and treatment and person centred care.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always effective

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always make sure people’s care and treatment were effective because they did not always ensure that Welcome House – The Chestnuts was the most suitable place for people to live. People told us one person moving in had caused them to feel uncomfortable and we read from the records that the person who moved in suffered regularly from anxiety and agitation towards others. This had resulted in some people being harmed.

In addition, this person required 1 to 1 staffing throughout the day and 2 to 1 when going out which meant that other people’s opportunity to go out had been impacted. This demonstrated this person’s needs had not been fully assessed prior to them moving into the service.

We found the funding authority’s assessments included in people’s care plans, together with the registered manager’s initial assessment. Information from both of these formed the basis of the person’s care plan.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always assess people’s capacity to make decisions around living at the service and their care. They did not always follow the principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 to determine if someone had capacity to make these decisions alone.

We found some capacity assessments in people’s care plans, but these did not cover all aspects of a person’s care. For example, one person was determined to have capacity and rightly staff did not carry out any other capacity assessments with this person. However, a second person was determined as lacking capacity to take medication or receive assistance with personal care, but there were no further capacity assessments completed, for example, around living at a service with 24-hour care or for the locked cupboards in the dining room. And although staff told us everyone had the capacity to make their own decisions this was not immediately clear from people’s care documents.

Staff understood the need to ask for a person’s consent prior to providing care. This meant in some instances people refused support and staff respected this. Staff understood people had the right to go out alone if they wished and told us, “We encourage people to make choices. They choose if they wash and what to wear.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always plan or deliver people’s care and treatment with them, taking into account any national guidance.

There was little evidence of staff supporting people to develop life skills to enable them to work towards living on their own, or achieving goals and aspirations, and there was nothing to show that staff were offering bespoke or therapeutical support to people, whether internally or from external professionals.

We spoke with the registered manager about national guidance to support people who had a mental health condition. They told us they were not aware of any and did not access any support groups or peer groups for advice and support, other than professionals such as the GP, psychiatrist or mental health nurse. Although later they said they referred to NICE guidance, they were unaware of charities such as MIND or Talking Therapies who may be able to support them to support people living at the service.

People were encouraged however to attend dental appointments, chiropodist appointments and visit the GP when required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager and staff worked well across teams and services to support people.

When people first moved into the service there was a lot of input from external health professionals and services such as the mental health team, psychiatry, social workers and the GP.

Where people had lost weight staff made referrals to the dietician and in the case of one person who had a choking incident, the speech and language therapy team were involved. A visiting professional told us, “They (staff) contact us in time and when needed.”

Other people were supported to attend appointments with the GP, diabetic eye screening service, dental community team and chiropodist.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always routinely monitor people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They did not always ensure that outcomes were positive and

consistent, or that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.

The registered manager and staff improved the outcomes for some people as some people had experienced harm or abuse prior to moving into Welcome House – the Chestnuts. Others were also at risk of self-neglect. Through staff’s input and care, people had started to accept support in their personal care and were living in an environment which was comfortable and much safer for them. People had clothing provided for them and for some people it was their first opportunity in a long time to sleep in a proper bed.

Staff training ensured positive outcomes for people. One person suffered a choking incident and it was through a staff member’s quick thinking, competency and training that they were able to carry out CPR whilst they waited for the ambulance. This resulted in the person recovering unharmed.

However, not everyone consistently experienced positive outcomes which met agreed expectations as set out in legislation, standard and evidence based clinical guidance as there were not structured approaches in place to improve people’s lives to enable them to attain their goals or aspirations.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager and staff did not always ensure people would be supported in relation to their health as care plans were not always clear.

One person’s stated they needed to have 2 glasses of full fat milk in the morning and at dinner if they agreed and yet, in another part of their care plan, it stated they did not like milk. This was part of their fluid and nutrition goal, but it was difficult to determine what this goal was.

Other documentation, which would be important if a person was admitted to hospital, had not been updated for some time. For example, one person’s hospital passport (a document that provides healthcare professionals with essential information about a person’s individual needs and preferences) had not been reviewed since 2021. This included information that this person was on insulin for their diabetes which was no longer the case. Another person’s was written in 2022.

However, staff recognised when people required professional healthcare input to maintain their health. For example one person was put on milkshakes by the GP following weight loss and this had helped to stabilise their weight. Another person was under the dietician when they needed support with their nutrition.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive

Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Requires Improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained Requires Improvement. This meant people’s needs were not always met.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person-centred care.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always responsive

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There were some shortfalls in how the registered manager and staff understood the diverse health and care needs of people. There was little improvement in people’s lives since our last inspection as once again, there was little going on for people.

Although staff provided a caring service to people, there was little evidence that people were being supported to integrate back into the community. We discussed the support one person received with cooking and were told by a staff member, “It is the basics like chopping veg because she loses interest, so they have not done anything more complex.” There was no clear plan, gauge or review of this person’s current cooking skills to determine what support they needed and as such staff had not considered if this was why the person may be losing interest.

A second person wished to move back to their flat and had told staff of this. However, there was no plan for staff to help the person work towards this. A staff member told us they spent time with this person on a 1 to 1 to achieve their goals, but there was no evidence of what these goals were, and from the daily records there was no evidence this person was doing anything other than watching television.

There was no evidence of a coordinated approach across care services to support people. Although professionals were involved, we did not read any multi-disciplinary meetings having taken place so staff could work together to enable people to ingrate back into society.

Some people were, however, supported with continuity by staff. This included 1 person who was supported to participate in their religious activities during the week and some other people who were encouraged and supported to see friends or family members.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not make sure that people could access the care and support they wished. One person told us, “I like going shopping, but I can’t always go out because of staff, especially if they are short staffed. It doesn’t happen a lot, but it does happen. I went out yesterday so I won’t go out today. I can only go out on certain days. I don’t have the opportunity go out in the evening. I would like to go to the restaurant down the road. I used to go there a lot.”

No specific goals were identified for people despite some people having expressed a wish to live independently again. The care plan for one person noted they required support with daily living skills, including learning to cook. However, there was no evidence this support had been put in place.

Staff did not also think creatively about how to support people with daily living tasks. For example, one person told us they were not allowed in the kitchen to make their own drinks. Staff explained this was because the person used a walker and could not carry a hot drink safely. However, they had not explored alternatives such as a kettle tipper, a perching stool, or adaptive two-handled mugs. They had also not considered starting with simple, achievable tasks and gradually introducing more complex steps as the person’s confidence and ability grew.

People were not encouraged or motivated to access external services or the community and nor did staff actively facilitate this. A staff member told us, “We encourage people to get out into the fresh air when it is nice.” However, they confirmed they meant the garden, rather than out in the community.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders did not actively listen to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes. This meant people’s care was not always tailored in response to this.

Staff used weekly ‘activity planners’ and staff told us they followed these to ensure people went out, or spent their time doing something meaningful to them. However, they also told us external outings usually consisted of walks and several people went out at the same time, so there appeared little opportunity for people to spend time on individualised activities of their choice. Despite these planners being in place, upon review of the daily notes for 6 people over a period of 3 weeks, we found only 3 people had been out on one occasion each. The other 3 people had spent their time indoors watching television or doing colouring.

One person’s planner showed they should go out 6 days a week for a walk, go to McDonalds and to the cinema, then on a Sunday they would bake. But their daily notes viewed from 23 July to the first day of inspection contained no evidence this was happening.

Throughout our first visit, people spent most of the day sat doing nothing. They were in the lounge watching television or in the dining area either eating or doing an activity such as a game or colouring.

In addition, although people were offered the opportunity to go out once a year with people from the provider’s other services, these outings were largely staff-led. Rather than seeking people’s ideas and discussing options together, staff pre-selected the outings and then presented 3 choices to people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff encouraged people to participate in the running of the service through conversation and feedback.

The registered manager told us they held in-house meetings with people so they had the opportunity to raise any concerns or ideas for outings and activities. They told us staff would then make arrangements to meet their needs and choices. They said, “We have service user meetings and they air their views and if they do not wish to speak in front of others they can come to the office and speak to me privately.” They told us they had added another option to the menu through one person’s feedback. We did not see any evidence, other than in meeting minutes, of people raising concerns or complaints and those being recorded and investigated by the registered manager. This was despite people telling us they would like to go out in the evening and would like the opportunity to be more involved in daily life skills such as cooking and baking. This showed that although the registered manager held in-house meetings, people’s views were not always fully taken into account and used as a basis in which to establish routines or practices that develop people as an individual.

They also told us that each year there was an external outing which people from all of the provider’s 5 services could participate in. They said, “They have a choice of 3 places to go and we organise the trip to the place most people choose. This year it is Margate.” This demonstrated an institutionalised practice within the service as although people were involved in choosing 1 of 3 options, there was not opportunity for them to make their own suggestion of where the annual trip was.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager and staff did not always make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices.

Although people’s care plans were very lengthy, they were detailed and gave a good level of information on how people ended up living at the service and the care they required. A staff member said, “I think they (care plans) are helpful. If people’s needs change or new habits become regular, we’d change the care plan to reflect this.”

Care plans were essentially up to date with people’s needs, care requirements and likes and dislikes. There was a good overview of a person’s personal history to help staff get to know people or understand why people may suffer from anxiety or agitation.

Yet, although there was supporting information for staff, we did not see this put into practice. For example, to support one person’s mental health, staff were encouraged to keep them engaged in meaningful daily activities, take them to the park for fresh air and involve them in cooking and meal preparation through one-to-one support. But there was no evidence this was happening and the person told us they had not been encouraged to cook, but would like to do so.

Although people had keyworkers who met with them to review their care plans, the notes from these discussions were largely task-focused, covering areas such as general well-being, personal care, oral hygiene, room cleaning and finances. There was little evidence of exploring social, emotional, or developmental needs or individual goals, preferences or aspirations. This meant, that although people were receiving the day to day care they required, opportunities for people to achieve outcomes beyond basic care needs were missed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life.

There was some information in people’s care plans about the end of their life and their wishes. For example, one person had stated which prayer they wanted, the music they wished played, and where they would like their funeral service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered did not always supply appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.

We asked the registered manager how they ensured information was presented in a way that could be understood for people. They were not really able to answer us as they said, “We let people know through one to one’s any changes that are going to be made, like the weather conditions – if it is going to be very hot.” However, after giving examples and clarifying what we meant by presenting information in a pictorial format, they confirmed that in-house meetings were documented in this way.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe

Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question Requires Improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to Inadequate. This meant people were not safe and were at risk of avoidable harm.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to people’s safe care and treatment, particularly in relation to accidents and incidents, infection control and medicines. They were also in breach of regulations in relation to staffing levels, failure to submit notifications of incidents. and safeguarding service users from abuse.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not assess or manage the risk of infection.

On our first visit the service was not clean and there was an unpleasant smell in parts. Touchpoints around light switches, door handles and handrails needed cleaning and there was ingrained dirty marks on doors and walls. The walls in one person’s room were covered in stains and splashes and their sink was not clean.

There were areas which created a trap for bacteria such as a cracked bathroom window, missing bath tap cap, chipped bath enamel and toilet which required de-scaling. The carpet in the hall downstairs was thick with dirt on the steps and sticky and there was also a similar patch on the carpet upstairs. The laundry room sink was also very dirty.

Cleaning schedules for the service were signed as being up to date, these included stating touchpoints had been cleaned. However, the bathroom schedules had not been signed since 7 August 2025. We asked the senior staff member for up-to-date schedules but they were not found.

On our second visit, the registered manager told us, “I have deep cleaned the house since your visit.” They stated that the cleanliness issues had been identified during their monthly walkaround audit. However, on review we noted that this audit was completed on 4 August 2025, before our first visit to the service on 12 August 2025. We also reviewed the July audit, which raised no concerns about cleanliness. Although we noted the provider’s quality assurance manager had identified some concerns in their July audit, these had not been actioned. This highlighted a lack of robustness in the infection control audit process.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not always provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

The registered manager and staff mostly worked with people to understand and manage risks. One person told us, “I feel fairly safe.” A second said, “I feel safe. I think it’s because of the staff.”

Documentation relating to people’s risks had improved since our last inspection and it was evident staff knew people well. We found clear guidance for staff on how to manage each person’s individual risks. For example, for people who experienced seizures, staff were provided with step-by-step instructions on how to respond and when to call the emergency services. For people at risk of self-neglect, care plans included sensitive and personalised information on the most effective ways to support or encourage them to accept help with personal care. Where people smoked, they were encouraged to give their cigarettes and lighter to staff at night and to participate in regular fire drills. There was a dedicated smoking area outside so people did not smoke indoors.

However, although these improvements were in place to support risk management through guidance and direction for staff, the registered manager had not fully considered the potential risks to people arising from some people’s anxiety and distress.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always have a proactive and positive culture of safety. Lessons were not always learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Although the registered manager recorded accidents and incidents, including descriptions and actions taken, incidents continued to occur because there was no robust follow-up to ensure staff learned from them. The registered manager confirmed they did not carry out any analysis of accidents and incidents to look for trends, themes or triggers. This meant they and staff were not always able to learn from incidents occurring in the service.

For example, one person frequently became distressed and attempted to harm others. Despite this pattern, the recorded action was simply that staff should ensure the person was not left alone when awake during the day. However, incidents persisted, and records showed occasions when the person was left unsupervised. On the day of inspection, one inspector spent 15 minutes talking to this person upstairs without any staff present.

This demonstrated the registered manager had failed to implement and monitor agreed safety measures, putting people at ongoing risk of harm.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not make sure that staff followed best practice in relation to medicines management.

Medicines were stored safely however staff checked the temperature of the medicine cabinet in each person’s room in the morning only, and we read on days the temperature was close to 25 degrees. This meant that staff would not know if the temperature had risen further at the hottest part of the day as they were not rechecking it. Despite discussing this with staff, on our second visit to the service, we found staff had not introduced a second temperature check of the cabinets.

There was no book for medicines being returned. A medicine returns book is crucial for maintaining accurate records of returned or expired medications, ensuring proper disposal.

Records relating to medicines were not accurate which meant the registered manager could not be assured people were receiving the medicines they required. One person’s medicine administration record (MAR) was handwritten and incorrect in places and one medicine was not clearly marked on the MAR, although staff amended this during the inspection. We carried out a stock count of this medicine and there were 82 in stock, however the records showed there should have been 56. The senior staff member said the discrepancy was due to the old stock not being returned at the end of the last month. However without a return’s book it was not possible to check the accuracy of this.

The ‘as and when’ (PRN) protocol for one person did not include information in line with NICE guidance. There was no information on what the medicine was expected to do and the minimum time between doses if the first dose had not worked. PRN medicines were being given regularly, rather than just as and when, and on one occasion a PRN was administered 4 times during the day, when the maximum dosage was 3 tablets in a day.

People’s medicine folders were untidy and not well maintained. One person was prescribed a pain patch. This was administered once a week and needed to be placed on a different part of their body each time. Although staff held a body map which showed where they had placed the pain patch each week, which was good practice, we found that although June and July’s records were in the person’s folder, there was nothing after that until 25 August 2025 meaning there was no record for the first 3 weeks of August. Staff told us initially that the form had been archived and they would look for it, however later a staff member found it in amongst the person’s daily care notes which were held in a totally different folder in a different room. Holding accurate, well-maintained records in relation to a person’s medicines is important to ensure that people were receiving safe care.

Only suitably trained and competency-assessed staff administered medicines to people. We checked the records for all staff and found they had either recently completed medicine refresher training, or had been competency checked by the registered manager (who was train the trainer in medication).

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always make sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff on duty each day, although staff told us they felt there were enough of them.

People told us they would like to go out more but they were restricted because of the staffing levels. One person said, “I went out yesterday, so I won’t go out today because there are not enough staff.” Another told us, “I would like to go out more.” Other people said they could not go out every day because of the staffing levels. There were 4 staff on duty each day to care for 13 people, one of whom required 1 to 1 staffing throughout the day and 2 to1 staffing when going out. It meant that many of the external outings for people were generally organised as a group as there were insufficient staff to accompany people individually. On our second visit to the service, 6 people had gone out together, with 2 staff.

Staff said they received good training. A staff member said, “The training is good. It’s mainly on DVD. We do the Care Certificate (an identified set of standards for health and social care professionals), we do competency assessments for medicines.”

If staff needed more training, they redid modules and in addition to training, staff had the opportunity to meet with their line manager on 1 to 1 basis through supervision. Staff told us they found this useful.

Staff were recruited through a robust process which included them providing evidence of their performance in their last role, their right to work in the UK and their fitness for the role. Prospective staff also went through a Disclosure and Barring Service check to help ensure they were suitable to work at this type of service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always detect and control potential risks in the environment.

Although the home provided suitable individual and communal spaces for people, the registered manager had not fully considered safety in relation to the garden. Outside on our first visit, we observed a disused washing machine, a wooden pallet and broken chairs. A metal panel with sharp edges was placed on top of the washing machine. While no one was recorded as being at risk of self-harming, the presence of these hazards posed potential risks, particularly as people were living with mental health conditions. When we went to the service on our second visit we found the garden had been tidied up as the provider’s quality assurance manager had identified we had concerns about it and had fed this back to the registered manager.

Other elements of the service were safe. For example, regular fire drills were carried out with the involvement of everyone living at the service, fire safety checks were completed, electrical checks carried out, and equipment such as the bath hoist was serviced regularly.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not manage or monitor people’s safety when people moved between different services.

One person had moved into the service several months ago. Although they had visited the service once beforehand, other people living there told us they had not been invited to take part in the decision for them to move in, and there was no evidence any further consideration had been given to whether people would be happy living together. As a result, some residents told us they felt, “uncomfortable” in their own home as the new person often became distressed and agitated, which disrupted the household. On our second visit to the service, the registered manager told us this person had been given notice and would be moving out in September. This demonstrated that the assessment process was not sufficiently robust to ensure that people’s needs could be met prior to them moving into the service. Although the registered manager told us, “We were not told everything (by the social worker) and when I went to assess [the person] they were calm. If we had known what we do now….”

A second person was noted as preferring it when other people were not around, as they did not like to be around many people. And yet, they lived in a service where a further 13 people resided. Although they visited the day before they moved in and records state, ‘it went well’ it is clear from the person’s care plan they do no not like to be with others.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not work well with people to understand what being safe meant to them or protect their right to live in safety, free from abuse or avoidable harm. The registered manager did not share concerns quickly and appropriately. We asked the registered manager if they had reported any of the incidents that had happened this year to the local safeguarding team. They told us, “I tell KCC (Kent County Council) about them, but I don’t do a referral. If there was a major incident I would inform CQC.” This demonstrated the registered manager’s lack of understanding on how to recognise abuse and how to report it.

We reviewed the service’s accident and incident records from 11 February 2025 to the first day of inspection. Fourteen incidents were recorded, 7 of which met the threshold for safeguarding referrals. However, these had not been reported to the local authority safeguarding team or the CQC, as required. As a result, the registered manager and provider could not be assured that people were safe living in the service.

Staff did understand what constituted safeguarding and reported incidents internally but there was a lack of robust systems and processes in place to ensure these were escalated appropriately. They were able to identify concerns, with one staff member telling us, “It can be about people’s changing behaviour, isolation, cuts and bruises, etc. I am comfortable (if I did identify something) the manager would do something about it. If nothing is done, I would speak to CQC.” Yet, although staff felt this, there was no evidence that concerns had been raised with the appropriate teams.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led

Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Requires Improvement. At this assessment the rating has changed to Inadequate. This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in leadership. Leaders and the culture they created did not assure the delivery of high-quality care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to good governance.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their organisation.

Staff said the provider visited the service regularly and that if something needed to be, “sorted” it was done. A staff member said, “I do feel valued here.”

Despite this, we found the registered manager and staff had not considered ways to give people more support to help them to achieve their goals and aspirations. The provider had fostered a closed culture within the service, where safeguarding concerns were managed internally rather than being appropriately escalated and insular practices limited transparency and accountability.

In addition, the provider had supported staff to work exceptionally long hours without adequate breaks. This placed staff at risk of fatigue and stress as well as increasing the likelihood of mistakes happening. It also meant people were at risk of receiving care from staff who were too tired to perform their roles safely and effectively.

The registered manager did not understand their role as a registered person as they had failed to notify CQC of incidents, accidents or safeguarding concerns which is a requirement of registration.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff felt they could speak up and that their voice would be heard. Staff told us, “I feel I am listened to. If nothing is done about concerns, I would speak to head office.”

Despite staff telling us this and that their voice would be heard, we found a poor culture in which institutionalised practices went unchallenged by the provider, leaders and staff. The registered manager told us they listened to staff concerns, and staff confirmed this. However, we could find no records of any concerns being raised regarding the issues we found at our inspection, and leaders and staff displayed no insight into how a perpetual culture of people’s concerns about their safety and well-being were not listened to.

We found no evidence of positive action being taken to improve people’s lives: the registered manager told us “I have 1 to1 chats with staff. I ask them if they have any problems and they can call me at any time. I pop in at weekends to check staff are okay.” Although this demonstrated the registered manager listened to staff and checked they were ‘okay’, there was no focus on people, or a recognition that people relied on staff and leaders to advocate for them when they themselves were unable to.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability or good governance.

We identified shortfalls in the governance arrangements during our last inspection and although the provider told us of the improvements they would make, we found this had not been done. Despite audits being carried out and staff keeping ‘check lists’ we found these were not being filled in accurately. For example, the cleaning check lists had not identified all the dirty areas in the service. We saw the provider’s QA (quality assurance) manager had written in their June audit, ‘pull cords need cleaning’, we found on our first day of inspection they were dirty. In addition, neither the provider’s QA manager nor the registered manager had identified through their monthly audits the inappropriate condition of the garden with the unsuitable items in it.

The provider’s action plan from our last inspection stated they would improve the opportunity for people to go out and yet, we found this had not happened. People still remained at risk of social isolation and without the support to attend activities or participate in pastimes meaningful to them.

In addition, although the provider’s QA manager had identified in July that in-depth cleaning of carpets were required in the service and gave a deadline of the following day, when we arrived on our first day of inspection on 12 August, we found this had not happened. We also read that the QA manager had identified on 2 consecutive months the registered manager had not completed their internal audit, despite being reminded to do so.

The registered manager told us on our second day, “I have cleaned the house from top to bottom since your visit and cleared the rubbish from the garden. The decorator is coming tomorrow to paint all the internal walls. I identified all of these areas from my last audit. I gave the maintenance man a list yesterday.” However, when we reviewed their audit, it was dated 4 August 2025 and stated, ‘house deep cleaned’. Yet we visited 8 days later and found this was not the case.

We also looked at the list given to the maintenance person and noted this had not included the cracked bathroom window, missing bath tap cap or chipped bath enamel.

We read the registered manager carried out unannounced out of hour checks. However, they did not maintain robust notes from these as we saw in one they had written they arrived at the service at 07:40 but left at 07:30.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider and senior staff did not focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation.

We asked the registered manager what changes had taken place to improve the service following our last visit. They told us, “Rooms have been decorated. We are doing more stuff with the residents and we have had a whole new staff change. The [provider’s QA] redeployed all staff around the other homes and we had a whole new staff team.” We asked if people were included in any consultation around this and the registered manager confirmed they were not.

Despite the provider sending us their action plan following our last inspection telling us how they planned to address the shortfalls, we found they had failed to make the required improvements.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not understand their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people.

The registered manager told us, “We work with health care professionals and some people go to church on a Sunday. We encourage everyone to attend church.” We asked about opportunities for people to engage in local groups or activities and they told us, “There is a day centre in Gillingham, I am going to look at the activities there for people and there is another group (I can’t remember the name) and I am going to try and get them in there.”

In addition, we asked about the opportunity for people to go out in the evening, for example to the pub or the cinema. The registered manager told us, “People don’t drink. They just don’t like going out at night. But I can arrange for the cinema – that’s a good idea.” This was despite one person telling us they would like to go for meal in the evening to their favourite restaurant.

This showed opportunities for people to engage in local groups were not already identified or embedded into daily practice. It also demonstrated a lack of will for staff to look at ways of working in partnership with the community for the benefit of people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There was a closed culture at the service. A "closed culture" is a poor culture that can lead to harm, including human rights breaches and abuse. We found a poor culture across the service, which had an ongoing detrimental impact on people’s safety and well-being: this had not been recognised or addressed by the registered manager or provider. The registered manager and provider did not have a clear shared vision, strategy and culture which was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. They did not always understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

The registered manager and staff told us they had a clear shared vision. However, this did not transfer into reality for people living at the service, and we found widespread concerns regarding people’s safety, including people experiencing being harmed. Leaders and staff did not always understand the challenges and the needs of people so they could ensure this was embedded into their daily practice so people were given the best opportunity to living fulfilling lives

Staff told us, “We work well together and the team is supportive of each other. We are here to help support and encourage people to be as independent as possible.” However, we found that people were not receiving person-centred care that offered variety, meaningful engagement, or opportunities to learn new skills to support their progress and enhance their quality of life.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Although the registered manager told us they valued diversity in their workforce. They were unable to give us any real example of how they, as the registered manager ensured inclusivity and fairness. This was demonstrated through the on-call arrangements within the service which we identified through staff rotas. This meant that on alternate weeks 1 staff member worked long hours between a Monday and Friday and were on call for the whole 7 days of that week. The registered manager had no pursued different options of sharing the on-call amongst the rest of the staff team or with staff of some of the provider’s other services which did not reduce pressure on individual staff.

Staff however felt the registered manager recognised diversity within the team. One told us, “If I needed adjustments, I am sure they would be in place. We have had staff before who were Muslim and they were supported to pray whilst at work.”

The registered manager told us, “We don’t discriminate; we treat everybody equally. We have different cultures within the staff team and different cultures within the service users.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Welcome House - The Chestnuts
asgRatings.name: Care Homes
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of Inspection: 15 September 2026 to 22 September 2026. Welcome House- The Chestnuts is a residential care home registered to support up to 15 people living with a mental health diagnosis. Not everyone supported by this service received the regulated activity of personal care. This assessment looked at people’s personal care and support. At the time of our assessment, the provider was supporting 11 people of whom 6 received the regulated activity of personal care.

The inspection was conducted to follow up an inspection in August 2025 where the service was rated “Inadequate” and multiple breaches of regulation identified. Following this inspection, the rating has changed to “Requires Improvement”. Although improvements in the quality and safety of care had been made, we identified repeated breaches of regulation in relation to person-centred care, dignity and respect, safe care and treatment and good governance.

We have assessed the service against ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ (RSRCRC) guidance to make judgements about whether the provider guaranteed people with a learning disability and autistic people respect, equality, dignity, choices, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted. At the time of the assessment, the service was supporting a small number of people with a learning disability. The provider had not fully considered ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ to ensure people received care that was person-centred or supported them to overcome barriers faced in society.

People were not consistently empowered to achieve any goals and aspirations through the care they received. Although some people had goals around living independently in the future, gaining voluntary employment or maintaining personal relationships, there was no clear plan of how this could be achieved. Leaders and staff were not consistently aware that people had any goals, or the support they might need to achieve these.

The model of care did not promote people’s independence. Even though most people could undertake some level of daily tasks for themselves and expressed enjoyment in doing so, there was little evidence that this was happening or that people were being supported to learn skills.

People’s physical health needs were met well, and there were appropriate levels of guidance and monitoring to support people’s health and wellbeing. Where people’s health needs changed, appropriate advice was sought and referrals made to ensure they could be supported safely.

There were sufficient staff employed to support people, who were safely recruited and appropriately training to support people’s needs. They were knowledgeable about people’s wellbeing and about their responsibilities to safeguard people from harm.

People were treated with kindness, however interactions were largely task based rather than staff spending quality time with people or discussing their wellbeing. There had been an increase in activities since our last inspection, but these were largely undertaken as groups and did not always reflect people’s abilities or social needs. There was lack of consideration as to individual wishes and preferences such as around activities and food, or how people could be empowered to participate in their wider community or culture. There was limited evidence around how people had been involved in reviewing their care to ensure it continued to meet their wishes.

The environment was largely well maintained, however the standard of cleanliness continued to fall below expectations in certain areas. Risks were posed to people through smoking in the building which had not been well assessed or monitored.

There were a system of audits and checks on the quality of care, but these were not always effective and had not identified areas found within our inspection.

There was no Registered Manager in position at the time of our inspection. Whilst the leadership arrangements had embedded some improvements, leaders themselves were not always knowledgeable about people or had a clear vision for the service. There was a lack of clear focus on best practice mental health care, or how care could be delivered holistically to ensure people had the best possible quality of care.

The service was previously placed into “Special Measures” which is an enhanced level of monitoring due to risks to the safety of people. Following this inspection, sufficient improvements have been made, and the service has been removed from special measures. However, we have requested an action plan from the provider setting out the steps they will take to ensure further improvements are made.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is not performing as well as it should and we have told the service how it must improve.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
We received varied feedback about people’s experience of living at The Chestnuts. People and relatives told inspectors that the care being delivered had improved since the last inspection, that there was a greater variety of activities and that leaders were approachable. One relative told us “The new manager has introduced an activities timetable which is much better and trying to do more activities outside the home. I’m happy at the moment and the manager is approachable with an open door policy, and is open to suggestions”. A person living at the service echoed this and explained “The staff are good. There is nothing that could be better at the moment”. A professional working with the home noted “The manager has changed and I have seen a fair more happier home, with the residents and staff seeming to be happy.

However, the care people received was not clearly tailored to their wishes, abilities or needs. It did not promote people’s independence, choice or support them to achieve any goals or aspirations from life. There were elements of care that were not person-centred or gave people control over the day in a way that reflected them as adults. One person told us “We all wake up early, at 6. The staff come and tell you it’s breakfast. We all go for breakfast”. Another person added “I want to move. We are treated like children”.

Although improvements in people’s experience were noted, we identified the quality of care being delivered continued to fall below the expected standards.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to Requires Improvement. This meant people did not always feel well-supported, cared for or treated with dignity and respect.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred-care and dignity and respect.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always caring

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always promote people’s independence

Although several people had expressed goals of living independently in the future, there was no clear structured plan of how staff would work with them to develop the skills they needed to do so. There was limited evidence of people being supported to do tasks for themselves such as assisting with meal preparation or tidying their rooms, despite it being recorded that some people enjoyed doing so. The arrangements at the service didn’t always promote meaningful choice or consider this as an opportunity to develop skills and independence. For instance, lunchtime and evening meals were served from a buffet where service users were called up one at a time to help themselves rather than being directly involved in the preparation. The majority of people we observed would have identical or very similar options, and the menu although developed alongside people was only changed seasonally.

There were some positive opportunities to maintaining people’s independence, such as supporting people to manage their finances safely and shopping trips where people were supported by staff to buy items they required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always treat people with kindness, empathy and compassion or respect their privacy and dignity.

Whilst individual interaction by staff members and people were kind, the organisational culture did not always treat people with dignity. People were not supported to have independence or control, or to achieve their goals or aspirations. Some areas of care were undignified, for example a smoking shelter being outside people’s bedrooms meaning noise and smoke would drift in. This had been identified at the last inspection but not addressed. The garden was littered with cigarettes and we observed a staff member pouring a bucket of cigarettes out into the garden.

People fed back that they had good relationships with their care staff, and enjoyed spending time with them. One person told us “It’s very good. They (staff). are very understanding when I get down”. We observed staff singing and dancing along with people during karaoke which brought enjoyment to all involved.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always take the time to listen to and understand people’s needs, views and wishes.

Whilst we observed staff interacted with people in a way that was kind and compassionate, the majority of these interactions were based on a task such as personal care or asking if people wished to have a drink. There was a lack of evidence of staff taking the time to sit and chat to people about their day, wishes or wellbeing despite the majority of people being described as requiring daily on weekly check in’s. This was especially important given the service supported people with a mental health diagnosis, where such informal conversations are important to monitor people’s mental health as well as bringing wider social and emotional benefits.

However, where people had support needs through their wider health and care needs, this was responded to in a timely way. For example, any deterioration in people’s physical health was quickly identified and a referral made to ensure they received the care they needed. Although most people’s mental health was stable, staff could explain to us how they would respond in a way that was personalised to each person if they were to become anxious or distressed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always treat people as individuals or make sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. They did not always take account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

Although there had been an increase in activities available to people, these continued to take place primarily as a group rather than considering each person’s wishes holistically and what they may wish to do individually. For example, there had been a recent trip to Margate alongside people who received care from other locations operated by the same provider. The location had been chosen as it was the most popular from all the people living at these services, and had been an annual trip for many years. Whilst it was positive to see people having this opportunity, we saw that several people had expressed wishes to go elsewhere and that they wouldn’t feel comfortable travelling by coach or to busy location. There was no evidence that it had been explored how they could go to these places by themselves, and experiencing the social and emotional benefits of discovering somewhere new or returning to a place that brought them meaning.

There was a heavy reliance on activities such as colouring in sessions as a group, which did not reflect people as adults or that they had abilities to do more challenging and enriching activities. However during our visit we also observed a karaoke session, which was very popular and brought clear enjoyment and joy to people. Some people were supported to do more individualised activities such as religious worship or maintain their personal appearance in a way which was appropriate to their culture.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff.

Staff told us they felt supported by leaders, who cared about their welfare and would encourage them to develop professionally including those who aspired to be leaders themselves in the future. One staff member told us “I feel very supported. The provider supported me through my education, and now to do training courses that I have requested to develop my skills. I am happy here”.

All staff received regular opportunities meet with managers, which always started with a discussion about their own welfare, and any factors in their personal life which they could be supported with support their wellbeing and their ability to work. When new staff joined the service, they told us this was a positive process which gave them opportunity shadow other staff and learn the needs of people before they started working with them. One member of staff told inspectors “I enjoy working with the people here and I have no concern. When I joined, I got lots of support and the induction was really good”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Requires Improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained Requires Improvement. This meant the effectiveness of people’s care, treatment and support did not always achieve good outcomes or was inconsistent.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always effective

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure people’s care and treatment were effective because they did not always check and discuss people’s health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

Although people’s needs were assessed, the level of guidance in place did not provide a consistent or clear plan of the care they should receive. The service were supporting people living with complex and enduring mental health conditions, however guidance primarily referred to medication and input from health professionals to manage this, rather than any actions staff could do proactively to promote their emotional wellbeing.

The quality of information in people’s care planning had improved since the last inspection and the provider had recently switched to digital records, but it was still not always clear that these were up to date or reflective of current needs. For example, one person was recorded as not liking meat but their care notes showed them eating this most days indicating that this was not the case.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

We observed that staff sought consent before performing any care tasks, which was clearly recorded within people’s daily care notes as well being seen in practice during our inspection. Staff were trained and knowledgeable about the principles of consent, and the rights of people to make their own choices. Where people were assessed as lacking mental capacity to make decisions, a best interest meeting was held with people’s representatives to make decisions on their behalf to ensure their welfare.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not plan and deliver people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them.

The model of care at The Chestnuts did not reflect best practice for a service supporting individuals with complex mental health needs. Guidance in place remained inconsistent about how people’s welfare could be promoted, and there was limited evidence that people had regular opportunities to discuss their wellbeing with staff or that this was proactively offered. The service had not considered wider factors such as promoting independence, meaningful social activity and person-centred goals that could promote people’s mental health, alongside any medical support or medication they received to manage this.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well across teams and services to support people.

We observed that staff treated people with kindness and were generally knowledgeable about how to keep them safe and support their physical health needs. However, there were significant inconsistencies in staff understanding around people’s goals and aspirations, and there was little evidence of staff working collaboratively to support people in achieving them or to improve their independence.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always routinely monitor people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They did not always ensure that outcomes were positive and consistent, or that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.

Although people’s physical health outcomes were largely monitored well, there was a lack of consistent monitoring of people’s wider social outcomes and what they wanted to achieve from their time at The Chestnuts. There was a lack of detailed plans of how people would be supported to achieve any goals or aspirations, and no evidence that these were being reviewed alongside people and adjusted accordingly. Keyworker meetings were taking place but the records of these were largely identical from month to month or did not reflect a detailed discussion with each person about their care.
