However, where people were at risk through malnutrition or dehydration staff were ensuring that people’s food and drink intake were being monitored, as well as their weight regularly checked. For people who had conditions such as diabetes we saw their blood sugar levels were being monitored regularly, to allow staff to intervene if these were to become unsafe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

People were able to access a range of health services both within and outside of the home. This included visits from services such as opticians and chiropodists on a regular basis, as well as attending appointments with the GP or mental health services which staff supported people to attend. Where people were less comfortable with leaving the building to attend appointments, staff had worked with people to improve their confidence. We identified one person had been reluctant to leave the building, however staff would now ensure they made them aware of the appointment well in advance to provide them with reassurance and they were now attending these in person which was a major step for them. One person told us “I went out this morning to have a blood test. Staff went with me”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Requires Improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained Requires Improvement. This meant people’s needs were not always met.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person-centred care
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always responsive

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There were some shortfalls in how the provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was not always joined-up, flexible or supportive of choice and continuity.

People were supported by a consistent staff team, who were kind and knowledgeable about their health needs. However, they did not all have the same understanding of what people wanted to achieve from living at The Chestnuts, or a coherent plan to help them to achieve these goals. People came from diverse backgrounds and cultures, however these were not always clearly reflected in their care or understood by leaders and staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it.

People were not able to access regular person-centred engagement, activity or support that was tailored to them to allow them like empowered lives focused on their skills and abilities. However, people were able to access health support when required. For people who might be reluctant or less able to leave the home, this included access home visits from health care professionals whilst those who could attend in person were supported by staff to do so. If people’s health and care needs deteriorated, this was responded to appropriately, so people received the support they needed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders did not always actively listen to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes. This meant people’s care was not always tailored in response to this.

The provider had not fully considered barriers faced by people with a mental health diagnosis in wider society, and how people could be supported to overcome these. For instance, people had goals around living independently, getting paid or voluntary employment or forming a relationship but there was no clear plan of how this would be achieved. We saw some consideration had been given to how people from diverse cultures could be supported to access care that promoted their culture and heritage, but again this had not been fully considered or demonstrated in practice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff did not always involve people in decisions about their care or tell them what had changed as a result.

Opportunities were not always taken to involve people in their own care, to ensure it continued to be shaped around the wishes and preferences. Although there were service user meetings which were well attended and discussed matters such as activities and food, these were not taking place frequently. There had only been 3 meetings between March 2026 and the date of our inspection, and 1 of these had been a very brief meeting to discuss the location of the summer trip. People had monthly keyworker meetings, however the records from these were largely identical each month and were primarily written about people rather than with them. There was also no clear evidence that people had been involved in writing their own care plan.

The provider did undertake annual surveys to gather the feedback of people, relatives and professionals who worked with the home. This feedback was mostly positive and where areas for improvement were identified, these were implemented in practice. All those we spoke with told us that any concerns they raised would be listen to by leaders, although there had been few complaints within the last year. One person told us “I could speak to (Manager name). She is nice”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not always work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs.

We saw some examples of person-centred care being undertaken, however there were further opportunities missed to ensure the care people received fully reflected them as an individual. For example, one person had a religious faith and were being supported to attend their place of worship regularly. However, there was no written guidance to help staff who were unfamiliar with their faith understand what it meant to them, or how they wished to be supported. We identified that certain staff had refused to enter their place of worship with them because of their own religion, which the provider hadn’t fully explored with staff as to why they might be uncomfortable doing. There was no reference to if they wanted to be supported to attend local religious festivals, and we noted they were largely eating the same food as their peers despite it being recorded they would like more food from their culture.

Likewise, another person was from a different culture and was supported to have their hair cut in a specialist hairdressers to reflect their heritage. However, there was no other guidance on their culture and how they may wish to express this, or consideration of how they could be supported to participate in their own community.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were not supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life.

There was no consistent or personalised plan setting out how staff should work with people to support them to achieve any future goals, such as living independently once more. There were multiple people who were described in their care plans as having aspirations to live in their own home in the future, however there was no detailed plan setting out how the service would work with them to equip them with the skills to do so. The majority of staff we spoke with stated there was either nobody who could live independently, or gave us the names of other service users where their care plan did not contain any references to independent living. One staff member told us “Everybody is fine here. Nobody has a goal to live by themselves”. Some people living at the service were in romantic relationships, however there was no guidance of any sort to describe how they may wish to be supported to maintain or develop these relationships or to ensure they were safe for both partners.

However we identified people had been supported to put in place end of life care plans in case their health were to deteriorate, which included references to spiritual or religious wishes and people they would like to be involved on their behalf.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.

We saw information was provided in easy read formats where required including activities timetables, minutes of meetings and copies of their keyworker reports to ensure people were able to process information in a way that was personalised to them. Staff communicated patiently with people, and would repeat things if needed and give people time to respond to ensure they had time to process information and make decisions for themselves.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to Requires Improvement. This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to safe and care treatment
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always assess or manage the risk of infection. They did not always detect and control the risk of it spreading or share concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

Although cleanliness had improved since our last inspection, it still remained inconsistent and people were not always supported in an environment that was clean or safeguarded them from the risk of infection. Kitchen surfaces such as cupboards and worktops were sticky to the touch, as were surfaces in certain people’s bedrooms. Some people had cobwebs and dust in their rooms indicating further work was needed to implement the improved standard of cleanliness throughout all parts of the building. However, staff worked alongside people to support them in manage their own personal hygiene to reduce the risk of infections. There was clear guidance in place of how this could be supported for each person, and people were supported to take pride in their appearance.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not always provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

Risks to people were not always managed safely or effectively. The people living at the service had diagnosis of complex mental health conditions. Although people’s emotional needs were largely stable, there was a continued lack of clear guidance on how staff should respond in a person-centred way if they were to become anxious or distressed to ensure their wellbeing and safety. For example, signs that a person might be struggling with their emotions were recorded but not how staff should respond if they were to observe these signs.

However, risks posed to people’s physical health were more consistently managed, for example around management of diabetes and risks posed to people with reduced mobility. There was clearer guidance and monitoring in these areas to ensure people’s safety.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Incidents at The Chestnuts were infrequent, however when they happened, they were investigated and reported appropriately. An investigation was undertaken to identify any contributory factors and learning that could be taken. We saw this was shared with staff, who had an up-to-date knowledge of how people should be supported safely in line with their current needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences.

Medication management systems were not effective at ensuring people would receive the medication they needed, when they needed it. The service was using multi-compartment compliance aids (MCA’s) in the form of blister bags for all people. These are not recommended by National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) due to the increased risk of medication errors, and that medication does not come with crucial safety information such as side effects. This meant we could not be assured staff would have this information available to refer to. During our inspection we identified some concerns about the temperature medications were being stored at meaning they would be less effective. This had been identified at our previous inspection and remained a concern.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs.

There were sufficient staff to support people’s needs safely, who were generally knowledgeable about each person and the care they received. There were robust recruitment systems in place to ensure all staff were suitable to work at The Chestnuts. This included the use of Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks, which are checks against the police national computer to help providers make safer recruitment decisions. Staff received regular supervisions to monitor their knowledge, abilities and welfare. Where more complex tasks were performed such as administering medications, staff had their competency assessed to ensure they were able to do so safely.

There were a small minority of staff who had not completed specific training around mental health. However we found in all other areas, staff had training that reflected the needs of the people they supported. Staff we spoke with could describe how they would support the physical and mental needs of people in their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. They did not always make sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

We identified evidence of people smoking with the building which was not being adequately controlled. The homes most recent independent fire risk assessment stated that people did not smoke within the building, which we identified was not accurate. Although there were controls agreed with people on access to cigarettes, these were not providing effective as it was still happening. There was an outdoor smoking area however this was located outside people’s bedroom windows, which did not reflect consideration to impact this might have on people in these rooms.

The environment was generally in a good state of maintenance, with regular checks taking place around utilities such as electricity, water, gas and fire safety. There were some remaining hazards such as a bathroom where the light was not functioning, and an unlocked boiler cupboard which was very hot to the touch. These were addressed following the inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.

There was appropriate guidance and monitoring in place to support people with their complex health needs, and we saw that referrals were made in a timely way when people’s health and wellbeing changed. For example, we saw staff had identified concerns about one person losing weight and had made a referral to the dietician. They were prescribed supplements and regular snacks as a result and had now returned to a stable and healthy weight.

There were systems in place to assess the needs of any people moving into the service to ensure they could be safely met; however nobody had moved into The Chestnuts since our previous inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately.

Staff were knowledgeable about their responsibilities to safeguard those in their care from the risk of abuse and neglect. They could confidently describe what signs of concern they may look out for, and what they would do if they were worried that a person was at risk of harm. One staff member told us “I would look out for any bruises, evidence of money being stolen, note changes in behaviour such as people not eating. I would report to my manager and take action to remove the person from danger if needed. If appropriate I could also speak to the local authority, police or CQC to share my concerns”. There had been no safeguarding incidents recently which required reporting to the local authority. People felt safe and one person told us “Yes, I do feel safe. The staff are kind and treat me well”.

People can only be deprived of their liberty to receive care and treatment when this is in their best interests and legally authorised under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA). In care homes, and some hospitals, this is usually through MCA application procedures called the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS). We checked whether the service was working within the principles of the MCA, whether appropriate legal authorisations were in place when needed to deprive a person of their liberty, and whether any conditions relating to those authorisations were being met. Where the risks to people were deemed sufficient that restrictions such as living in locked accommodation were needed, to ensure their safety, appropriate authorisations were sought and recorded.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to Requires Improvement. This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to good governance.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Leaders did not understand context in which the provider delivered care, treatment and support. They did not embody the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders did not have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively.

Although people and partners we spoke to had noted some improvements had been made by the manager, they did not have a clear vision for the service or knowledge of the people being supported. They had a limited understanding and focus on how people’s mental welfare could be promoted holistically through choice, independence and meaningful activity. We identified that a number of areas continued to fall below the standards expected or reflect best practice care for individuals living with a mental health diagnosis. The manager was not knowledgeable about the people being supported, and when asked to tell us about people stated they had only been at the service for 6 months so did not know people well. Some elements of care such as around activities, food and daily living tasks remained institutionalised and did not consider how people could be challenged to take positive risks.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider developed a culture where people could speak up and their voice would be heard. However, we could not always see this had happened in practice.

Staff felt comfortable about being able to raise concerns openly, and these would be listened to and acted upon. One staff member told us “I can definitely can speak to my manager or senior carer. They are very open”. Another staff member echoed this and told us “I like the manager. She is very approachable”. Despite this, we identified that people continued to live lives that did not reflect their diverse needs, interests or aspirations. They were not consistently treated with dignity or supported to gain in independence, grow and develop in skills and wellbeing. There was no evidence that this had been identified, and there remained a culture that did not focus on the people in their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability or good governance. They did not act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate.

There was a regular schedule of audits and checks to ensure the ongoing quality of care, however these were not as effective as they needed to be. They did not consistently ensure the safety of the building, level of cleanliness, accuracy of care documentation or that a clear plan was in place for how people could be supported to achieve their goals and aspirations. Spot checks by provider representatives were undertaken in addition to those completed by the manager, and although they were identifying areas for improvement these had not all been realised at the inspection. For individuals with a learning disability and autistic people, the provider had not fully considered the principles of RSRCRC to ensure they receive care that was person-centred and promoted independence.

There was a business continuity policy to cover any emergencies such as the loss of an important utility or extreme weather event to ensure people would have continuity of care. There was also an on-call system where there was always a management representative available to respond in urgent situations.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not always encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people.

Although areas of care delivery had improved since the inspection, it had not yet reached the standard that we would expect. There had been additional training for staff around mental health and a consultant had worked with the service to review care planning documents, but the care being delivered still did not reflect a holistic model that considered all factors that could promote people’s emotional wellbeing.

There were very few incidents recorded at the service, however that that we saw were investigated well and appropriate action taken. This learning was shared within staff meetings, handovers and individual supervisions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

The service worked closely with partners in their local community to support the needs of people, which included supporting regular appointments with health services for routine checkup’s and if staff were concerned about people’s welfare. Health and care professionals who shared feedback with us spoke of positive relationships with the home. One stakeholder told us “I have a good relationship with the staff and management. They always make me feel welcome”. The provider also worked to form relationships with wider community groups, including mental health support groups which were attended by people regularly, as well as local places of worship.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have a clear shared vision, strategy and culture which was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. They did not understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities.

There was no clear vision both for the service as a whole, and for what individual people wanted to achieve from living at the service. Although staff and leaders were kind, they had no holistic plan for each person around aspirations or goals and how they could be achieved. People generally participated in activities together and there was a lack of exploration of individual cultures, wishes and preferences. Tasks were generally done on behalf of people with limited evidence of independence and choice being encouraged, or of a clear focus on enabling people to have the best possible quality of life.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

The provider and leaders ensured that staff were treated equally at the work place, and considered how barriers faced by the diverse workforce could be overcome to improve their experience at work. Where people needed to work flexibly around personal commitments such as children, family or any health needs this was supported. One staff member had recently been unwell for a period of time, and spoke highly of the support and care they received from their manager and colleagues. They stated “I got great support from my colleagues and manager. They all rallied round me, and even arranged a video call with the people who I care for which was a nice touched as they were worried having not seen me. It’s a lovely place to work”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
